solution: The component along an axis is the magnitude times the cosine of the angle to that axis. Here $F_x = F\cos\theta = (240\ \text{N})\cos 35^\circ = 197$ N. The vertical component, $240\sin 35^\circ = 138$ N, plays no role in this question.

name: Two-leg walk
statement: A hiker walks $4.0$ km due east, then $3.0$ km due north. What is the magnitude of her net displacement, in kilometres?
solution: Displacements add as vectors, so add components and then take the magnitude. The net displacement is $(4.0\,\hat{\imath} + 3.0\,\hat{\jmath})$ km, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{4.0^2+3.0^2} = 5.0$ km. Note that this is less than the $7.0$ km of path length walked.

name: Work from a dot product
statement: A constant force $\vec{F} = (12\,\hat{\imath} - 5\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a box while the box undergoes a displacement $\vec{d} = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ m. How much work does the force do, in joules?
solution: Work is the dot product $W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$, computed component by component. $W = (12)(3) + (-5)(4) = 36 - 20 = 16$ J. The force has a component opposing part of the motion, which is why the answer is much smaller than $|\vec F||\vec d| = 65$ J.

name: Angle between two pulls
statement: Two ropes pull on a ring. One exerts $\vec{A} = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ N and the other $\vec{B} = (4\,\hat{\imath} + 3\,\hat{\jmath})$ N. What is the angle between the two forces, in degrees?
solution: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{|\vec A||\vec B|}$. Here $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 12+12 = 24$ and $|\vec A| = |\vec B| = 5$, so $\cos\theta = 24/25 = 0.96$ and $\theta = 16.3^\circ$.

name: Length of a 3D displacement
statement: A drone flies from the origin to the point $(2, 3, 6)$ m. How far is it from the origin, in metres?
solution: The magnitude of a three-dimensional vector is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$. $\sqrt{4+9+36} = \sqrt{49} = 7.0$ m.

name: Vertical component of a launch
statement: A ball is thrown at $25$ m/s at an angle of $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. What is the vertical component of its initial velocity, in m/s?
solution: The component perpendicular to the reference axis uses the sine. $v_y = (25\ \text{m/s})\sin 40^\circ = 16.1$ m/s. This is the piece that determines how high the ball rises.

name: Wrench on a bolt
statement: A mechanic pushes on a wrench with a force of $80$ N at a point $0.25$ m from the bolt. The force makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the wrench handle. What is the magnitude of the torque about the bolt, in N$\cdot$m?
solution: $|\vec\tau| = |\vec r\times\vec F| = rF\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the handle and the force. $\tau = (0.25)(80)\sin 60^\circ = 17.3$ N$\cdot$m. Only the component of $\vec F$ perpendicular to the handle twists the bolt.

name: Making two vectors perpendicular
statement: For what value of $k$ are the vectors $\vec{A} = 3\,\hat{\imath} + k\,\hat{\jmath} - 2\,\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B} = 4\,\hat{\imath} + 5\,\hat{\jmath} + 1\,\hat{k}$ perpendicular? Give the value of $k$ (dimensionless).
solution: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product vanishes. $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 12 + 5k - 2 = 0$, so $5k = -10$ and $k = -2$.

name: Drifting across a river
statement: A boat points straight across a river and moves at $4.0$ m/s relative to the water. The river current is $3.0$ m/s downstream. What is the boat's speed relative to the bank, in m/s?
solution: Velocities add as vectors: $\vec v_{bank} = \vec v_{water} + \vec v_{current}$. The two are perpendicular, so the speed is $\sqrt{4.0^2 + 3.0^2} = 5.0$ m/s.

name: Change of velocity around a corner
statement: A car travelling at $12$ m/s due east turns and ends up travelling at $12$ m/s due north, without changing speed. What is the magnitude of its change in velocity, in m/s?
solution: $\Delta\vec v = \vec v_f - \vec v_i$ is a vector difference, not a difference of speeds. With $\vec v_i = 12\,\hat{\imath}$ and $\vec v_f = 12\,\hat{\jmath}$, $\Delta\vec v = (-12\,\hat{\imath} + 12\,\hat{\jmath})$ m/s, of magnitude $12\sqrt2 = 17$ m/s. The speed is unchanged but the velocity certainly is not.

name: Component along a diagonal
statement: A force $\vec{F} = (5\,\hat{\imath} + 12\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a bead that is constrained to slide along a wire pointing in the direction $\hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath}$. What is the component of $\vec F$ along the wire, in newtons?
solution: The component of $\vec F$ along a direction is $\vec F\cdot\hat u$, where $\hat u$ is a unit vector. Here $\hat u = (\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath})/\sqrt2$, so $\vec F\cdot\hat u = (5+12)/\sqrt2 = 17/\sqrt2 = 12.0$ N. Forgetting to normalise $\hat u$ is the usual mistake.

name: Steering to land straight across
statement: A river $80$ m wide flows at $2.0$ m/s. A swimmer can swim at $5.0$ m/s relative to the water and wants to land at the point directly opposite her starting point. At what angle upstream from the straight-across direction must she aim, in degrees?
solution: To have zero net downstream velocity, the upstream component of her swimming velocity must cancel the current. That requires $v\sin\theta = u$, so $\sin\theta = 2.0/5.0 = 0.40$ and $\theta = 23.6^\circ$. The width of the river does not affect the aiming angle, only the crossing time.

name: Plane in a crosswind
statement: A small plane holds a heading due north with an airspeed of $180$ km/h. A steady wind of $50$ km/h blows from the west toward the east. What is the plane's ground speed, in km/h?
solution: Ground velocity = air velocity + wind velocity, and here the two are perpendicular. The ground velocity is $(50\,\hat{\imath} + 180\,\hat{\jmath})$ km/h, so the ground speed is $\sqrt{50^2+180^2} = 187$ km/h. The plane is also blown $50$ km/h off course to the east.

name: Area of a triangular plate
statement: A flat triangular plate has corners at $A = (0,0,0)$, $B = (2,3,1)$ and $C = (1,-1,4)$, with coordinates in metres. What is the area of the plate, in m$^2$?
solution: The magnitude of a cross product is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, so a triangle has area $\tfrac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}|$. Here $\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC} = (13, -7, -5)$, whose magnitude is $15.59$, giving an area of $7.79$ m$^2$.

name: Magnetic force on an ion
statement: An ion of charge $q = +2.0\ \mu$C moves with velocity $\vec v = 3.0\times10^{5}\,\hat{\imath}$ m/s through a magnetic field $\vec B = (0.50\,\hat{\jmath} + 0.20\,\hat{k})$ T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it, in newtons?
solution: $\vec F = q\,\vec v\times\vec B$. With $\vec v$ along $\hat{\imath}$, $\vec v\times\vec B = 3.0\times10^{5}(0.50\,\hat{k} - 0.20\,\hat{\jmath})$, of magnitude $1.616\times10^{5}$ m$\cdot$T/s. Multiplying by $q = 2.0\times10^{-6}$ C gives $F = 0.323$ N.

name: Torque from a 3D position vector
statement: A force $\vec F = 50\,\hat{k}$ N is applied at the point $\vec r = (0.30\,\hat{\imath} + 0.20\,\hat{\jmath})$ m relative to a pivot. What is the magnitude of the torque about the pivot, in N$\cdot$m?
solution: Compute $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ component by component. $\vec\tau = (0.20)(50)\,\hat{\imath} - (0.30)(50)\,\hat{\jmath} = (10\,\hat{\imath} - 15\,\hat{\jmath})$ N$\cdot$m, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{10^2+15^2} = 18.0$ N$\cdot$m.

name: Third force for equilibrium
statement: Three forces act on a small ring and hold it in equilibrium. One is $30$ N pointing along the $+x$ axis; another is $40$ N pointing $120^\circ$ counterclockwise from the $+x$ axis. What is the magnitude of the third force, in newtons?
solution: In equilibrium the three forces sum to zero, so the third equals the negative of the sum of the first two. The first two add to $(30 - 20)\,\hat{\imath} + 34.64\,\hat{\jmath} = (10, 34.64)$ N, so the third has magnitude $\sqrt{10^2 + 34.64^2} = 36.1$ N.

name: Angle to the vertical
statement: A cable pulls in the direction $\vec v = (4\,\hat{\imath} - 3\,\hat{\jmath} + 12\,\hat{k})$, where $\hat k$ points vertically upward. What angle does the cable make with the vertical, in degrees?
solution: The direction cosine with respect to an axis is the component along that axis divided by the magnitude. $|\vec v| = \sqrt{16+9+144} = 13$, so $\cos\theta = 12/13$ and $\theta = 22.6^\circ$.

name: Volume of a slanted box
statement: A parallelepiped is spanned by the edge vectors $\vec a = (2,1,0)$ m, $\vec b = (0,3,1)$ m and $\vec c = (1,0,4)$ m. What is its volume, in m$^3$?
solution: The volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$. Here $\vec b\times\vec c = (12, 1, -3)$, so $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c) = 24 + 1 + 0 = 25$, giving $25$ m$^3$.

name: Diagonal of a cube
statement: A crystal has a cubic unit cell. What angle does the body diagonal of a cube make with one of the cube's edges, in degrees?
solution: Take the cube of side $1$ with an edge along $\hat{\imath}$ and the diagonal along $(1,1,1)$. Then $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\theta = 54.7^\circ$. Every edge meeting that corner makes the same angle with the diagonal.

name: Work done by gravity on a ramp
statement: A $25$ kg crate slides $8.0$ m down a ramp inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. How much work does gravity do on the crate, in joules?
solution: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = mgd\cos\phi$, where $\phi = 60^\circ$ is the angle between the downward weight and the displacement along the ramp. Equivalently, only the drop in height matters: $W = mgd\sin 30^\circ = (25)(9.8)(8.0)(0.50) = 980$ J.

name: Two forces at an angle
statement: Two forces of $12$ N and $18$ N act at the same point with an angle of $50^\circ$ between them. What is the magnitude of their resultant, in newtons?
solution: $|\vec A + \vec B|^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta$, which follows from expanding the dot product of the sum with itself. Here $144 + 324 + 2(12)(18)\cos 50^\circ = 745.7$, so the resultant is $27.3$ N.

name: Crossing against a fast current
statement: A river $150$ m wide flows at $3.0$ m/s. A rower can row at only $2.0$ m/s relative to the water, so she cannot avoid being carried downstream. If she chooses her heading to make the downstream drift as small as possible, how far downstream does she land, in metres?
solution: With the boat slower than the current, minimise the drift-to-width ratio rather than the drift itself. If she aims at angle $\theta$ upstream of straight across, the crossing time is $w/(v\cos\theta)$ and the drift is $x = w\dfrac{u - v\sin\theta}{v\cos\theta}$. Setting $dx/d\theta = 0$ gives $\sin\theta = v/u = 2/3$, and substituting back gives $x = w\sqrt{u^2 - v^2}/v = 150\sqrt{5}/2 = 168$ m.

name: The perpendicular leftover
statement: A force $\vec F = (3\,\hat{\imath} + 4\,\hat{\jmath})$ N acts on a bead threaded on a straight rod pointing along $\vec d = (1,2,2)$. The rod exerts whatever transverse force is needed to keep the bead on it. What is the magnitude of the component of $\vec F$ perpendicular to the rod, in newtons?
solution: Split $\vec F$ into a piece parallel to $\hat d$ and the leftover. With $\hat d = (1,2,2)/3$, the parallel component is $\vec F\cdot\hat d = (3 + 8)/3 = 3.667$ N. Since $|\vec F| = 5$ N and the two pieces are perpendicular, the transverse part is $\sqrt{5^2 - 3.667^2} = 3.40$ N.

name: Closest approach of two ships
statement: At noon, ship B is $12$ km due east of ship A. Ship A steams east at $18$ km/h; ship B steams north at $10$ km/h. Treating both as points moving in straight lines, what is their distance of closest approach, in kilometres?
solution: Work in A's frame. The relative position of B is $\vec r_0 = (12, 0)$ km and the relative velocity is $\vec v_{rel} = (10\,\hat{\jmath}) - (18\,\hat{\imath}) = (-18, 10)$ km/h. The closest approach is the perpendicular distance from A to that straight line, $d = |\vec r_0\times\vec v_{rel}|/|\vec v_{rel}| = 120/20.59 = 5.83$ km, reached after about $0.51$ h.

name: Pushing a crate up a slope
statement: A $40$ kg crate rests on a frictionless ramp inclined at $25^\circ$. A worker pushes it with a $200$ N force directed horizontally, into the hill. What is the net force on the crate along the ramp surface, in newtons? Take a positive answer to mean the crate accelerates up the slope.
solution: Resolve both the horizontal push and the vertical weight along the ramp direction. The push contributes $200\cos 25^\circ = 181.3$ N up the slope; gravity contributes $mg\sin 25^\circ = (40)(9.8)\sin 25^\circ = 165.7$ N down the slope. The net along-ramp force is $181.3 - 165.7 = 15.6$ N, just barely up the slope.

name: Area of a parallelogram in space
statement: A flat solar panel is a parallelogram whose adjacent sides are $\vec a = (4, -2, 1)$ m and $\vec b = (1, 3, 2)$ m. What is the area of the panel, in m$^2$?
solution: The area of the parallelogram is $|\vec a\times\vec b|$. Computing, $\vec a\times\vec b = (-2\cdot2 - 1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot1 - 4\cdot2,\ 4\cdot3 + 2\cdot1) = (-7, -7, 14)$, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{49+49+196} = 17.1$ m$^2$.

name: Proton in a general field
statement: A proton ($q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C) moves with velocity $\vec v = (2.0\,\hat{\imath} - 1.0\,\hat{\jmath} + 3.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{6}$ m/s in a magnetic field $\vec B = (0.050\,\hat{\imath} + 0.10\,\hat{\jmath} - 0.020\,\hat{k})$ T. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on it, in newtons?
solution: Evaluate $\vec v\times\vec B$ by the determinant rule, then multiply by $q$. The cross product is $(-0.28, 0.19, 0.25)\times10^{6}$ in SI units, of magnitude $4.207\times10^{5}$. Multiplying by $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C gives $F = 6.73\times10^{-14}$ N.

name: Impact parameter of an alpha particle
statement: At a certain instant an alpha particle is at position $\vec r_0 = (3.0\,\hat{\imath} - 4.0\,\hat{\jmath} + 2.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{-12}$ m relative to a heavy nucleus, moving with velocity $\vec v = (2.0\,\hat{\imath} + 1.0\,\hat{\jmath} - 2.0\,\hat{k})\times10^{6}$ m/s. If the particle were undeflected and continued in a straight line, how close would it come to the nucleus, in metres?
solution: The impact parameter is the perpendicular distance from the nucleus to the straight-line path, and $|\vec r_0\times\vec v| = |\vec r_0||\vec v|\sin\theta$ picks out exactly the perpendicular piece. So $b = |\vec r_0\times\vec v|/|\vec v|$. Here $\vec r_0\times\vec v = (6.0, 10.0, 11.0)\times10^{-6}$ in SI units, of magnitude $1.603\times10^{-5}$, and $|\vec v| = 3.0\times10^{6}$ m/s, giving $b = 5.34\times10^{-12}$ m. Since $\vec r_0\cdot\vec v < 0$, the particle is still approaching, so this distance is actually reached.

name: Three cables holding a lamp
statement: A $500$ N lamp hangs at the point $P = (0,0,0)$ and is held up by three straight cables running to ceiling anchors at $A = (2, 0, 3)$ m, $B = (-1, 2, 3)$ m and $C = (-1, -2, 3)$ m. What is the tension in cable $PA$, in newtons?
solution: Each cable pulls along its own unit vector, and the three tensions plus the weight must sum to zero. Writing $\hat u_A = (2,0,3)/\sqrt{13}$, $\hat u_B = (-1,2,3)/\sqrt{14}$, $\hat u_C = (-1,-2,3)/\sqrt{14}$, the condition $T_A\hat u_A + T_B\hat u_B + T_C\hat u_C = 500\,\hat k$ gives three equations. Symmetry in $y$ forces $T_B = T_C$, and solving the remaining $x$ and $z$ equations gives $T_A = 200$ N (with $T_B = T_C = 208$ N).

name: Velocity from a quadratic position
statement: A cart moves along a straight track. Its position in meters is $x(t) = 3t^2 - 4t + 2$, with $t$ in seconds. Find the speed of the cart at $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$, in m/s.
solution: Velocity is the time derivative of position. $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 6t - 4$. At $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$, $v = 18 - 4 = 14\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Acceleration from a cubic position
statement: A bead slides on a wire with position $x(t) = 5t^3 - 2t$ (meters, seconds). Find its acceleration at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Acceleration is the second derivative of position. $v = 15t^2 - 2$ and $a = 30t$. At $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$, $a = 60\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Top of the ball's flight
statement: A ball is thrown straight up from the ground. Its height in meters is $y(t) = 20t - 4.9t^2$. How long after launch does it reach its highest point, in seconds?
solution: At the top of the flight the velocity is zero, so set $dy/dt = 0$. $v = 20 - 9.8t = 0$ gives $t = 20/9.8 = 2.04\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: When does the acceleration vanish?
statement: A particle's velocity in m/s is $v(t) = 8t - 3t^2$. At what time is its acceleration zero, in seconds?
solution: $a = dv/dt$. Here $a = 8 - 6t$, which is zero at $t = 8/6 = 1.33\,\mathrm{s}$. This is also the instant the particle is moving fastest.

name: Fastest point of an oscillation
statement: A mass on a spring oscillates with $x(t) = 0.50\sin(4.0t)$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds. Find its maximum speed, in m/s.
solution: Differentiate and read off the amplitude of the result. $v = (0.50)(4.0)\cos(4.0t) = 2.0\cos(4.0t)$, so the largest speed is $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, reached whenever the mass passes through $x = 0$.

name: How far out does it get?
statement: A trolley moves with $x(t) = 12t - t^3$ (meters, seconds), starting at the origin at $t=0$. Find the largest positive value of $x$ it reaches, in meters.
solution: The turning point is where $v = 0$. $v = 12 - 3t^2 = 0$ gives $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$. Then $x = 12(2) - 2^3 = 16\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Braking with exponential decay
statement: A boat's engine is cut and its speed decays as $v(t) = 30e^{-t/5}$ m/s, with $t$ in seconds. Find its acceleration at $t = 0$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (report the signed value).
solution: Differentiate the exponential using the chain rule. $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 30\left(-\tfrac{1}{5}\right)e^{-t/5} = -6e^{-t/5}$. At $t = 0$ this is $-6.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Speed on a circular track
statement: A stone is whirled on a string of radius $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Its angle from the $x$-axis is $\theta(t) = 0.50t^2$ radians. Find the stone's speed at $t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$, in m/s.
solution: For circular motion $v = R\,\frac{d\theta}{dt}$. Here $\dot\theta = t$, so at $t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$, $\dot\theta = 4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $v = (3.0)(4.0) = 12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Inflating balloon
statement: A spherical weather balloon is being inflated. At the moment its radius is $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$, the radius is growing at $0.020\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast is the volume increasing at that moment, in $\mathrm{m^3/s}$?
solution: Related rates through the chain rule. $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 \frac{dr}{dt} = 4\pi (0.50)^2 (0.020) = 0.0628\,\mathrm{m^3/s}$.

name: Tip of a walking shadow
statement: A street lamp holds a bulb $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above level ground. A person $1.8\,\mathrm{m}$ tall walks away from the base of the lamp at $1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$. How fast does the tip of the person's shadow move along the ground, in m/s?
solution: Similar triangles give a linear relation, then differentiate. If $x$ is the person's distance from the lamp and $s$ the shadow tip's distance, $\frac{1.8}{5.0} = \frac{s-x}{s}$, so $s = \frac{5.0}{5.0-1.8}x$. Differentiating, $\dot s = \frac{5.0}{3.2}(1.5) = 2.34\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Ladder sliding down a wall
statement: A $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its base is dragged away from the wall at a steady $0.40\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When the base is $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the wall, how fast is the top sliding down, in m/s?
solution: Differentiate the constraint $x^2 + y^2 = L^2$. This gives $x\dot x + y\dot y = 0$, so $\dot y = -x\dot x/y$. With $x = 3.0$, $y = \sqrt{25-9} = 4.0$, and $\dot x = 0.40$, the top moves down at $(3.0)(0.40)/4.0 = 0.30\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Acceleration from a speed-position graph
statement: A puck slides so that its speed depends on position as $v = 2.0\sqrt{x}$, with $v$ in m/s and $x$ in meters. Find its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: When speed is known as a function of position, use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$. Here $\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1.0}{\sqrt{x}}$, so $a = 2.0\sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{1.0}{\sqrt{x}} = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The motion is uniformly accelerated, which matches $v^2 = 2ax$.

name: Rocket at peak acceleration change
statement: A small rocket rises with velocity $v(t) = 500\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{t}{20}\right) - 9.8t$ m/s, where $t$ is in seconds. At what time is its acceleration zero, in seconds?
solution: Differentiate with the chain rule and set the result to zero. $a = \frac{500}{20+t} - 9.8 = 0$ gives $20 + t = \frac{500}{9.8} = 51.0$, so $t = 31.0\,\mathrm{s}$. This is when the rocket is moving fastest.

name: Winching a boat to the dock
statement: A winch on a dock sits $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above the point where a rope is tied to a boat's bow. The rope is reeled in at $0.50\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ of rope remain between winch and bow, how fast is the boat approaching the dock, in m/s?
solution: With $x$ the horizontal distance and $L$ the rope length, $x^2 + 2.0^2 = L^2$, so $x\dot x = L\dot L$. When $L = 5.0$, $x = \sqrt{25-4} = 4.583\,\mathrm{m}$, giving $\dot x = (5.0)(0.50)/4.583 = 0.546\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The boat moves faster than the rope is pulled.

name: Half-amplitude time of a damped swing
statement: A pendulum's swing amplitude decays as $A(t) = A_0 e^{-t/4.0}$, with $t$ in seconds. How long does it take the amplitude to fall to half its initial value, in seconds?
solution: The decay constant sets the rate, since $\frac{dA}{dt} = -A/4.0$. Solving $e^{-t/4.0} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ gives $t = 4.0\ln 2 = 2.77\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Closest approach of two cars
statement: At $t = 0$ a car leaves an intersection heading east at a constant $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. At the same moment a second car is $100\,\mathrm{m}$ north of the intersection, heading south toward it at a constant $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the smallest distance between the two cars, in meters.
solution: Minimize the squared separation, which avoids differentiating a square root. $D^2 = (20t)^2 + (100-15t)^2$; setting $\frac{d(D^2)}{dt} = 1250t - 3000 = 0$ gives $t = 2.4\,\mathrm{s}$. Then the separations are $48\,\mathrm{m}$ east and $64\,\mathrm{m}$ north, so $D = 80\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Speed for maximum engine power
statement: A motor pushes a sled with a force that drops with speed: $F = 4000 - 20v$ newtons, with $v$ in m/s. Find the maximum mechanical power the motor can deliver, in watts.
solution: $P = Fv$, so maximize $P(v) = 4000v - 20v^2$. Setting $\frac{dP}{dv} = 4000 - 40v = 0$ gives $v = 100\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $P = (4000-2000)(100) = 2.0\times 10^5\,\mathrm{W}$.

name: Equilibrium from a potential well
statement: Two atoms interact with potential energy $U(x) = \frac{6.0}{x^2} - \frac{4.0}{x}$, where $U$ is in joules and $x$ is the separation in meters. Find the separation at which the atoms are in equilibrium, in meters.
solution: The force is $F = -\frac{dU}{dx}$, and equilibrium means $\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$. Here $\frac{dU}{dx} = -\frac{12}{x^3} + \frac{4.0}{x^2} = 0$, so $x = 12/4.0 = 3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Since $U$ has a minimum there, the equilibrium is stable.

name: Lifeguard's fastest route
statement: A lifeguard stands on sand $40\,\mathrm{m}$ from a straight shoreline. A swimmer in trouble is $30\,\mathrm{m}$ out into the water, and $100\,\mathrm{m}$ down the beach measured parallel to the shoreline. The lifeguard runs at $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on sand and swims at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the shortest possible time to reach the swimmer, in seconds.
solution: Let the lifeguard enter the water a distance $x$ down the beach and minimize $T(x) = \frac{\sqrt{40^2+x^2}}{6.0} + \frac{\sqrt{30^2+(100-x)^2}}{2.0}$. Setting $dT/dx = 0$ is exactly Snell's law, $\frac{\sin\theta_1}{6.0} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{2.0}$, and gives $x = 90.4\,\mathrm{m}$. The resulting time is $32.2\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Rate of change of speed
statement: A drone's velocity components in m/s are $v_x = 3.0 + 2.0t$ and $v_y = 4.0$, with $t$ in seconds. How fast is its speed increasing at $t = 0$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$?
solution: The rate of change of speed is not the magnitude of the acceleration. Differentiating $|\vec v| = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ gives $\frac{d|\vec v|}{dt} = \frac{v_x a_x + v_y a_y}{|\vec v|}$. At $t=0$: $|\vec v| = 5.0$, $a_x = 2.0$, $a_y = 0$, so the answer is $(3.0)(2.0)/5.0 = 1.2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, less than $|\vec a| = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Fastest point on a rolling tire
statement: A bicycle wheel rolls without slipping along a road while the bicycle moves at $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Consider a small pebble stuck in the tread. Find the largest speed the pebble ever has relative to the road, in m/s.
solution: Superpose translation and rotation. A tread point has position $x = v t + R\sin(\ldots)$ type terms; differentiating the cycloid gives speed $2v\left|\sin\frac{\phi}{2}\right|$, where $\phi$ is the angle turned since the point touched the road. The maximum is $2v = 16\,\mathrm{m/s}$, at the top of the wheel; the bottom point is instantaneously at rest.

name: Drag that depends on position
statement: A dart fired into a thick gel slows according to $v(x) = 20e^{-0.050x}$, where $v$ is in m/s and $x$ is the depth in meters. Find its acceleration at depth $x = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (report the signed value).
solution: Use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ because speed is given versus position. $\frac{dv}{dx} = -1.0e^{-0.050x}$, so $a = -20e^{-0.10x}$. At $x = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, $a = -20e^{-1} = -7.36\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Acceleration of the ladder's top
statement: A $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ ladder leans against a vertical wall, and its base is dragged away from the wall at a constant $0.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$. When the base is $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the wall, find the magnitude of the acceleration of the ladder's top, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Differentiate the constraint twice. From $y = \sqrt{L^2-x^2}$, $\dot y = -x\dot x/y$, and differentiating again with $\ddot x = 0$ gives $\ddot y = -\frac{\dot x^2}{y} + \frac{x\dot x\,\dot y}{y^2}$. With $x=3.0$, $y=4.0$, $\dot x = 0.60$, $\dot y = -0.45$: $\ddot y = -0.090 - 0.0506 = -0.141\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so the magnitude is $0.141\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Best throwing angle off a cliff
statement: A stone is thrown at $25\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the edge of a cliff $30\,\mathrm{m}$ above flat ground. Choosing the launch angle to make the stone land as far from the base of the cliff as possible, find that maximum horizontal distance, in meters.
solution: Write the range as a function of the launch angle and maximize it. Flight time comes from $-30 = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2$, and $R(\theta) = v_0\cos\theta\,t$. Setting $dR/d\theta = 0$ gives $\theta = 35.7^\circ$, below $45^\circ$ because the extra drop rewards a flatter, faster horizontal throw. The maximum range is $R = 88.8\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: When does the projectile stop receding?
statement: A ball is launched from the origin at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $80^\circ$ above the horizontal. Its straight-line distance from the launch point does not increase monotonically. Find the first time at which that distance stops increasing, in seconds.
solution: The distance $r$ stops growing when $\frac{d(r^2)}{dt} = 2\vec r\cdot\vec v = 0$, i.e. when velocity is perpendicular to the position vector. With $x = v_0\cos\theta\,t$ and $y = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac12 g t^2$, dividing out the trivial root $t=0$ and solving gives $t = 2.14\,\mathrm{s}$. This happens only for steep launches, $\theta > 70.5^\circ$.

name: Chain sliding off a table
statement: A uniform chain of length $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ lies on a frictionless table with $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ hanging over the edge. Released from rest, how fast is the chain moving at the instant the last link leaves the table, in m/s?
solution: With $x$ the hanging length, the driving weight is $Mgx/L$ on total mass $M$, so $a = gx/L$. Write $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ and integrate: $\tfrac12 v^2 = \frac{g}{2L}(L^2 - x_0^2)$. Thus $v = \sqrt{gL\left(1 - x_0^2/L^2\right)} = \sqrt{(9.8)(2.0)(1-0.0625)} = 4.29\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Longest shot up a slope
statement: A ball is projected at $14\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from a point on a hillside that rises at $20^\circ$ to the horizontal. Choosing the launch direction to maximize the distance the ball travels along the slope before landing on it, find that maximum distance, in meters.
solution: In axes tilted with the slope, the range along the incline is $R(\theta) = \frac{2v_0^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$ measured from the horizontal launch angle $\theta$. Differentiating, the product of sines and cosines peaks at $\theta = 45^\circ + \alpha/2 = 55^\circ$, and then $R_{\max} = \frac{v_0^2}{g(1+\sin\alpha)} = \frac{196}{9.8(1.342)} = 14.9\,\mathrm{m}$.

name: Total acceleration on a banked oval
statement: A car starts a lap on a circular track of radius $200\,\mathrm{m}$ at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and speeds up steadily, its speed being $v(t) = 5.0 + 0.80t$ m/s. At what time does the magnitude of its total acceleration first reach $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, in seconds?
solution: The tangential part is $dv/dt = 0.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and the centripetal part is $v^2/R$, and they are perpendicular. Setting $\sqrt{0.80^2 + (v^2/200)^2} = 2.0$ gives $v^2 = 200\sqrt{4.0-0.64} = 366.7$, so $v = 19.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $t = (19.1-5.0)/0.80 = 17.7\,\mathrm{s}$.

name: Fastest-turning telescope
statement: A rocket lifts off from rest straight up with a constant acceleration of $20\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. An observer stands $800\,\mathrm{m}$ from the launch pad and tracks it with a telescope. Find the maximum rate at which the telescope's elevation angle must turn, in rad/s.
solution: With $y = 10t^2$ and $\tan\theta = y/800$, the chain rule gives $\dot\theta = \frac{800\,\dot y}{800^2 + y^2} = \frac{16000t}{640000 + 100t^4}$. Setting $d\dot\theta/dt = 0$ gives $300t^4 = 640000$, so $t = 6.80\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\dot\theta = 0.127\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Unlike the constant-speed case, the peak is not at liftoff, because the rocket starts too slow.

name: Cheapest shot to a target
statement: A cannon must hit a target that sits $40\,\mathrm{m}$ horizontally away and $15\,\mathrm{m}$ above the muzzle. Find the smallest launch speed that can reach the target, in m/s.
solution: Eliminate time to get the trajectory $y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}\sec^2\theta$, then solve for $v_0^2$ as a function of $\theta$ and minimize it. Differentiating gives the condition $\tan 2\theta = -x/y$, and substituting back yields the clean result $v_{\min}^2 = g\left(y + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right)$. With $x = 40$, $y = 15$: $v_{\min} = \sqrt{9.8(15+42.7)} = 23.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Trapezoid on a velocity-time graph
statement: A train starts from rest. Its velocity rises linearly from $0$ to $12$ m/s during the first $4$ s, stays at $12$ m/s until $t = 10$ s, then falls linearly to zero at $t = 14$ s. How far does the train travel in the full $14$ s? Give the answer in meters.
solution: Displacement is the area under the $v$-$t$ curve, $x = \int v\,dt$. The shape is a trapezoid: two triangles and a rectangle. $\tfrac12(4)(12) + (6)(12) + \tfrac12(4)(12) = 24 + 72 + 24 = 120$ m.

name: Area under an acceleration-time graph
statement: A cart starts from rest. Its acceleration is $+3.0$ m/s$^2$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 5.0$ s, then $-2.0$ m/s$^2$ from $t = 5.0$ s to $t = 11.0$ s. What is the cart's velocity at $t = 11.0$ s, in m/s?
solution: $\Delta v = \int a\,dt$, the signed area under the $a$-$t$ graph. First segment: $(3.0)(5.0) = 15$ m/s. Second: $(-2.0)(6.0) = -12$ m/s. Starting from rest, $v = 15 - 12 = 3.0$ m/s.

name: Work as area under a force-position graph
statement: A block is pushed along a straight track. The applied force is along the motion and rises linearly from $0$ to $20$ N over the first $3.0$ m, then stays at $20$ N until $x = 8.0$ m. How much work does the force do over the $8.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.
solution: $W = \int F\,dx$ is the area under the $F$-$x$ graph. Triangle: $\tfrac12(3.0)(20) = 30$ J. Rectangle: $(5.0)(20) = 100$ J. Total $W = 130$ J.

name: Work to stretch a spring
statement: A spring obeys $F = kx$ with $k = 250$ N/m. How much work must you do to stretch it from its natural length to $x = 0.12$ m? Give the answer in joules.

name: From a(t) to v(t)
statement: A particle starts from rest at $t = 0$ with acceleration $a(t) = 6t$ (SI units, $t$ in seconds). What is its speed at $t = 4.0$ s, in m/s?

name: Total charge from a ramping current
statement: The current through a wire grows as $i(t) = 0.40t$ amperes, with $t$ in seconds. How much total charge passes a cross-section between $t = 0$ and $t = 10$ s? Give the answer in coulombs.
solution: Charge is the integral of current, $q = \int i\,dt$. $q = \int_0^{10} 0.40t\,dt = 0.20t^2\big|_0^{10} = 20$ C.

name: Impulse from a growing force
statement: During a collision the force on a ball grows linearly as $F(t) = 50t$ newtons for $0 \le t \le 0.20$ s, then drops to zero. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered, in N$\cdot$s?

name: Work by a quadratic force
statement: A force along the $x$-axis has magnitude $F(x) = 8.0x^2$ newtons, with $x$ in meters. How much work does it do on an object moved from $x = 0$ to $x = 3.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.

name: Center of mass of a rod with linear density
statement: A thin rod of length $2.0$ m lies along the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 2.0$ m. Its linear mass density grows in proportion to distance from the left end: $\lambda(x) = cx$. How far from the left end is the center of mass, in meters?
solution: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int x\,\lambda\,dx}{\int \lambda\,dx}$. The constant $c$ cancels: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int_0^L x^2 dx}{\int_0^L x\,dx} = \dfrac{L^3/3}{L^2/2} = \tfrac{2}{3}L = 1.33$ m.

name: RMS of a sinusoidal voltage
statement: A household voltage varies as $V(t) = 170\sin(\omega t)$ volts. The RMS value is defined by $V_{rms}^2 = \dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^{T} V^2\,dt$ over one full period $T$. What is $V_{rms}$, in volts?
solution: The average of $\sin^2$ over a whole cycle is exactly $\tfrac12$. So $V_{rms}^2 = \tfrac12(170)^2$ and $V_{rms} = 170/\sqrt{2} = 120$ V.

name: Two integrations of a linear acceleration
statement: A cart starts from rest at the origin at $t = 0$ with acceleration $a(t) = 12 - 4t$ (SI units). How far from the origin is it at $t = 3.0$ s? Give the answer in meters.
solution: Integrate twice. $v(t) = \int_0^t (12 - 4t')dt' = 12t - 2t^2$, then $x(t) = \int_0^t v\,dt' = 6t^2 - \tfrac23 t^3$. At $t = 3$: $x = 54 - 18 = 36$ m.

name: Raising a satellite to twice the Earth's radius
statement: A $1200$ kg satellite is moved from the Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m) out to a radius of $2R$. Using $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, how much work must be done against gravity? Ignore the Earth's rotation and any kinetic energy. Give the answer in joules.
solution: Gravity weakens with distance, so $W = \int_R^{2R}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{2R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{2R}$. That gives $\dfrac{(3.986\times10^{14})(1200)}{2(6.37\times10^{6})} = 3.75\times10^{10}$ J.

name: Energy stored in a charging capacitor
statement: A $4.7\ \mu$F capacitor is charged from $0$ to $200$ V by a supply. The work to push the next increment of charge is $dW = (q/C)\,dq$. How much total energy ends up stored in the capacitor? Give the answer in joules.
solution: $W = \int_0^{Q}\dfrac{q}{C}dq = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C} = \tfrac12 CV^2$, since the voltage rises as the charge accumulates. $W = \tfrac12(4.7\times10^{-6})(200)^2 = 0.094$ J.

name: Lifting a chain off the floor
statement: A uniform chain of length $8.0$ m and mass per length $2.0$ kg/m lies coiled on the floor. You lift one end straight up until the whole chain hangs vertically, with its lower end just touching the floor. How much work do you do? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: The piece of chain that ends up at height $x$ has mass $\lambda\,dx$ and needs work $\lambda g x\,dx$. So $W = \int_0^{L}\lambda g x\,dx = \tfrac12 \lambda g L^2 = \tfrac12(2.0)(9.8)(64) = 627$ J. Equivalently, the center of mass rises to $L/2$.

name: Pumping a cylindrical tank dry
statement: An open cylindrical tank of radius $1.5$ m is filled with water to a depth of $3.0$ m, right up to the rim. Water has density $1000$ kg/m$^3$. How much work is needed to pump all of it out over the rim? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: A slab at height $y$ above the bottom has mass $\rho \pi r^2\,dy$ and must be raised $(3 - y)$. $W = \rho g \pi r^2 \int_0^{3}(3-y)\,dy = \rho g \pi r^2 (4.5)$. With $r = 1.5$ m this is $(1000)(9.8)\pi(2.25)(4.5) = 3.12\times10^{5}$ J.

name: Using v dv = a dx
statement: A bead starts from rest at $x = 0$ and its acceleration depends on position as $a(x) = 5.0x$ (SI units). What is its speed at $x = 4.0$ m, in m/s?
solution: When $a$ is given as a function of $x$, use $v\,dv = a\,dx$. Then $\tfrac12 v^2 = \int_0^{4} 5x\,dx = \tfrac52 x^2\big|_0^4 = 40$, so $v = \sqrt{80} = 8.94$ m/s.

name: Moment of inertia of a rod about its end
statement: A uniform thin rod has mass $3.0$ kg and length $1.2$ m. Find its moment of inertia about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod, by integrating. Give the answer in kg$\cdot$m$^2$.
solution: $I = \int r^2\,dm$ with $dm = (M/L)dx$. $I = \dfrac{M}{L}\int_0^{L} x^2 dx = \dfrac{ML^2}{3} = \dfrac{(3.0)(1.44)}{3} = 1.44$ kg$\cdot$m$^2$.

name: Coasting boat with linear drag
statement: A $1200$ kg boat moving at $6.0$ m/s cuts its engine. The water exerts a drag force $F = -bv$ with $b = 90$ N$\cdot$s/m. How far does the boat coast before (asymptotically) stopping? Give the answer in meters.
solution: Write $m v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -bv$, so $m\,dv = -b\,dx$. Integrating from $v_0$ to $0$ gives $x = \dfrac{m v_0}{b} = \dfrac{(1200)(6.0)}{90} = 80$ m. The boat never truly stops, but the total distance is finite.

name: Triangular acceleration pulse
statement: A rocket sled starts from rest. Its acceleration rises linearly from $0$ to $6.0$ m/s$^2$ over $0 \le t \le 3.0$ s, then falls linearly back to zero at $t = 5.0$ s. What is its speed at $t = 5.0$ s, in m/s?
solution: $\Delta v$ is the area under the $a$-$t$ graph, here two triangles. $\tfrac12(3.0)(6.0) + \tfrac12(2.0)(6.0) = 9.0 + 6.0 = 15$ m/s.

name: Work by an inverse-square-like force
statement: A repulsive force along the $x$-axis has magnitude $F(x) = \dfrac{200}{(1 + x)^2}$ newtons, with $x$ in meters. How much work does it do on a bead pushed from $x = 0$ to $x = 3.0$ m? Give the answer in joules.

name: Impulse from a half-sine force pulse
statement: A bat strikes a ball with a force that follows $F(t) = 80\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{T}\right)$ newtons for $0 \le t \le T$, where $T = 0.50$ s, and is zero otherwise. What is the magnitude of the impulse, in N$\cdot$s?
solution: $J = \int_0^{T} F_0 \sin(\pi t/T)\,dt = \dfrac{2F_0 T}{\pi}$. With $F_0 = 80$ N and $T = 0.50$ s, $J = \dfrac{2(80)(0.5)}{\pi} = 25.5$ N$\cdot$s.

name: Center of mass with quadratic density
statement: A rod of length $1.00$ m lies from $x = 0$ to $x = 1.00$ m with linear density $\lambda(x) = \lambda_0\left(1 + x^2\right)$, where $x$ is in meters. Where is its center of mass, in meters from the left end?
solution: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\int_0^1 x(1+x^2)dx}{\int_0^1 (1+x^2)dx} = \dfrac{1/2 + 1/4}{1 + 1/3} = \dfrac{0.75}{1.3333} = 0.563$ m. It sits right of center because the rod is heavier on the right.

name: Rocket speed with shrinking mass
statement: A rocket in deep space (ignore gravity) has initial mass $3000$ kg and burns fuel at a steady $15$ kg/s while its engine produces a constant thrust of $45{,}000$ N. Starting from rest, what is its speed after a $60$ s burn? Give the answer in m/s.
solution: The acceleration is not constant because the mass shrinks: $a(t) = \dfrac{F}{m_0 - kt}$. Then $v = \int_0^{t_b}\dfrac{F\,dt}{m_0 - kt} = \dfrac{F}{k}\ln\!\dfrac{m_0}{m_0 - kt_b}$. With $m_0 - kt_b = 3000 - 900 = 2100$ kg, $v = 3000\ln(3000/2100) = 1.07\times10^{3}$ m/s.

name: Chain sliding off a table
statement: A uniform chain of total length $6.0$ m and total mass $12$ kg lies on a frictionless table with $2.0$ m hanging over the edge. It is released from rest and slides off. How fast is it moving the instant the last link leaves the table? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in m/s.
solution: Track the potential energy of the hanging part, whose center of mass is $h/2$ below the edge: $U(h) = -\lambda g h^2/2$ with $\lambda = 2.0$ kg/m. From $h = 2$ to $h = 6$, $|\Delta U| = \tfrac12(2.0)(9.8)(36 - 4) = 313.6$ J. Then $v = \sqrt{2(313.6)/12} = 7.23$ m/s.

name: Pumping a conical tank
statement: A tank is a cone with its apex pointing down, height $4.0$ m and top radius $2.0$ m. It is full of water ($1000$ kg/m$^3$). How much work is required to pump all the water out over the top rim? Use $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$. Give the answer in joules.
solution: At height $y$ above the apex, the cross-section has radius $r = y/2$, so a slab has volume $\pi y^2/4\,dy$ and must rise $(4-y)$. $W = \rho g \dfrac{\pi}{4}\int_0^{4} y^2(4-y)\,dy = \rho g \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{4\cdot 64}{3} - \dfrac{256}{4}\right) = \rho g (16.76)$, giving $1.64\times10^{5}$ J.

name: Work to reach a 500 km orbit altitude
statement: How much work must be done against gravity to raise a $500$ kg payload from the Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m) to an altitude of $500$ km? Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ and neglect kinetic energy and air resistance. Give the answer in joules.
solution: $W = \int_{R}^{R+h}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac1R - \dfrac{1}{R+h}\right)$. With $R+h = 6.87\times10^{6}$ m, $W = (3.986\times10^{14})(500)(1.5699\times10^{-7} - 1.4556\times10^{-7}) = 2.28\times10^{9}$ J. Note $mgh$ would give $2.45\times10^{9}$ J, about 8% high.

name: Moment of inertia of a disk with graded density
statement: A flat disk of radius $0.50$ m and total mass $2.0$ kg has an areal density that grows with radius as $\sigma(r) = \sigma_0 r$. Find its moment of inertia about the central axis perpendicular to the disk, in kg$\cdot$m$^2$.
solution: Use rings, $dm = \sigma_0 r(2\pi r\,dr)$. Then $M = 2\pi\sigma_0 R^3/3$ and $I = \int r^2 dm = 2\pi\sigma_0 R^5/5$. Dividing, $I = \tfrac35 MR^2 = 0.6(2.0)(0.25) = 0.30$ kg$\cdot$m$^2$ — larger than $\tfrac12 MR^2$ because mass sits farther out.

name: Distance to halve speed under quadratic drag
statement: A skydiver of mass $80$ kg moving horizontally at high speed feels only a drag force $F = -cv^2$ with $c = 0.25$ kg/m (ignore gravity for this horizontal glide). Over what distance does the speed drop to half its initial value? Give the answer in meters.
solution: $m v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -cv^2$ gives $\dfrac{dv}{v} = -\dfrac{c}{m}dx$. Integrating, $x = \dfrac{m}{c}\ln\!\dfrac{v_0}{v} = \dfrac{80}{0.25}\ln 2 = 222$ m. Notice the answer does not depend on $v_0$.

name: Burnout altitude of a rocket fighting gravity
statement: A rocket lifts off vertically from rest with initial mass $6000$ kg, exhaust speed $u = 2500$ m/s, and a steady burn rate of $40$ kg/s for $100$ s. Its speed obeys $v(t) = u\ln\!\dfrac{m_0}{m_0 - kt} - gt$. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ constant, what altitude does it reach at burnout? Give the answer in meters.
solution: Altitude is $\int_0^{t_b} v\,dt$, and the logarithm integrates to $\int_0^{t_b}\ln\frac{m_0}{m_0-kt}dt = t_b + \dfrac{m_f}{k}\ln\dfrac{m_f}{m_0}$ with $m_f = 2000$ kg. That gives $u\left(100 + 50\ln\tfrac{2000}{6000}\right) - \tfrac12 g t_b^2 = 2500(45.07) - 49000 \approx 6.37\times10^{4}$ m.

name: Falling to Earth from three radii out
statement: A small object is released from rest at a distance $3R$ from the Earth's center, where $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m. Neglecting air resistance and the Moon, how fast is it moving when it reaches the Earth's surface? Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$. Give the answer in m/s.
solution: Gravity is not constant over this distance, so integrate the force: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = \int_{R}^{3R}\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}dr = GMm\left(\dfrac1R - \dfrac{1}{3R}\right) = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$. Then $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{4GM}{3R}} = \sqrt{8.34\times10^{7}} = 9.13\times10^{3}$ m/s, just below escape speed.

name: Restoring force on a small-angle pendulum
statement: A pendulum bob of mass $0.25$ kg hangs on a light string. The string is displaced $4.0^\circ$ from vertical. Using the small-angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (with $\theta$ in radians), find the magnitude of the restoring force along the arc, in newtons.
solution: The tangential force is $mg\sin\theta$, and for small $\theta$ in radians $\sin\theta\approx\theta$. Convert: $4.0^\circ = 0.0698$ rad. Then $F \approx mg\theta = (0.25)(9.8)(0.0698) = 0.171$ N. The exact value $mg\sin\theta = 0.1709$ N differs by less than $0.1\%$.

name: Gravity at 250 km altitude
statement: The gravitational field strength at height $h$ above Earth's surface is $g(h) = g_0\left(1+\frac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}$ with $R = 6.37\times10^6$ m. Use the binomial approximation $(1+x)^n \approx 1+nx$ to estimate the percent decrease in $g$ at $h = 250$ km. Give the answer in percent.
solution: With $x = h/R = 250/6370 = 0.03925 \ll 1$, $(1+x)^{-2} \approx 1-2x$. The fractional decrease is $2h/R = 0.0785$, i.e. $7.85\%$. (The exact value is $7.41\%$; the first-order estimate overshoots slightly because $x$ is not tiny.)

name: Fractional change in pendulum period
statement: A pendulum's length is increased by $0.60\%$. Using $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ and the binomial approximation, find the percent increase in the period.
solution: $T \propto L^{1/2}$, so writing $L \to L(1+x)$ gives $T \to T(1+x)^{1/2} \approx T(1+x/2)$. With $x = 0.0060$, $\Delta T/T = 0.0030 = 0.30\%$. Half-power laws always halve a small fractional change.

name: Fraction of a sample decayed in a short time
statement: A radioactive sample has half-life $12.0$ hours. Use $e^{-x} \approx 1-x$ for small $x$ to estimate the fraction of nuclei that decay in the first $6.0$ minutes. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: The surviving fraction is $e^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda = \ln 2/t_{1/2}$, so the decayed fraction is $1-e^{-\lambda t} \approx \lambda t$ when $\lambda t \ll 1$. Here $\lambda t = (\ln 2)(0.100\ \text{h})/(12.0\ \text{h}) = 5.78\times10^{-3}$. The exact answer, $5.76\times10^{-3}$, is within $0.3\%$.

name: How high does the bob rise?
statement: A pendulum of length $1.20$ m swings to a maximum angle of $6.0^\circ$ from vertical. Use $\cos\theta \approx 1-\theta^2/2$ to estimate how high the bob rises above its lowest point, in meters.
solution: The rise is $h = L(1-\cos\theta)$, and the leading term of $1-\cos\theta$ is $\theta^2/2$, not $\theta$. With $\theta = 0.1047$ rad, $h \approx L\theta^2/2 = (1.20)(0.01097)/2 = 6.58\times10^{-3}$ m. Note that the first-order term vanishes, so you must keep the quadratic term.

name: Gamma factor for a slow particle
statement: An electron moves at $v = 0.010c$. Use the binomial approximation on $\gamma = (1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ to estimate $\gamma - 1$. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: With $x = -v^2/c^2$ and $n = -1/2$, $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2}$. So $\gamma - 1 \approx \frac{1}{2}(0.010)^2 = 5.0\times10^{-5}$. The exact value agrees to four digits.

name: Area expansion of a metal plate
statement: An aluminum plate ($\alpha = 2.4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$) is heated by $80$ K. Each linear dimension grows by the factor $(1+\alpha\Delta T)$. Use the binomial approximation to find the fractional increase in the plate's area. Give a dimensionless number.
solution: Area scales as the square of a length, so $A \to A(1+\alpha\Delta T)^2 \approx A(1+2\alpha\Delta T)$. Thus $\Delta A/A \approx 2(2.4\times10^{-5})(80) = 3.84\times10^{-3}$. The dropped term $(\alpha\Delta T)^2 \approx 3.7\times10^{-6}$ is negligible.

name: Pendulum taken to a place with weaker gravity
statement: A pendulum clock is moved to a location where $g$ is smaller by $0.30\%$. By what percent does its period increase?
solution: $T \propto g^{-1/2}$, so $\Delta T/T \approx -\frac{1}{2}\Delta g/g$. A $0.30\%$ decrease in $g$ gives a $0.15\%$ increase in period. The clock runs slow by that fraction.

name: Laser spot shift from a small tilt
statement: A laser is aimed at a wall $8.0$ m away and then tilted by $0.25^\circ$. Use $\tan\theta \approx \theta$ to find how far the spot moves along the wall, in meters.
solution: The displacement is $d = L\tan\theta \approx L\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians. Here $\theta = 0.25^\circ = 4.363\times10^{-3}$ rad, so $d \approx (8.0)(4.363\times10^{-3}) = 0.0349$ m, about $3.5$ cm. At this angle $\tan\theta$ and $\theta$ agree to six digits.

name: Refraction at a small angle of incidence
statement: Light strikes a flat water surface ($n = 1.33$) at $3.0^\circ$ from the normal. Using $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ on both sides of Snell's law, find the refraction angle in the water, in degrees.
solution: Snell's law is $\sin\theta_1 = n\sin\theta_2$; for small angles this becomes $\theta_1 \approx n\theta_2$, and because the approximation is linear the angles may be left in degrees. So $\theta_2 \approx 3.0/1.33 = 2.26^\circ$, matching the exact result to three digits.

name: Second-order correction to kinetic energy
statement: A particle moves at $v = 0.050c$. Expanding $K = (\gamma-1)mc^2$ to the next order beyond $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ gives $K \approx \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1+\frac{3}{4}\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)$. By what fraction does the true kinetic energy exceed the Newtonian value? Give a dimensionless number.
solution: Keep two terms of $\gamma = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\beta^2 + \frac{3}{8}\beta^4 + \dots$, so $K = mc^2(\frac{1}{2}\beta^2 + \frac{3}{8}\beta^4)$ and the fractional excess over $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is $\frac{3}{4}\beta^2$. With $\beta = 0.050$, that is $\frac{3}{4}(0.0025) = 1.88\times10^{-3}$. Direct evaluation of $\gamma$ confirms $1.879\times10^{-3}$.

name: Tidal acceleration from the Moon
statement: The Moon ($M = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg) is $d = 3.84\times10^{8}$ m from Earth's center. Expanding $GM/(d\mp R)^2$ to first order in $R/d$, the tidal acceleration at the sublunar point relative to Earth's center is $2GMR/d^3$. Compute it, with $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m and $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The tide comes from the *difference* in field across Earth, and that difference is the derivative $\frac{d}{dr}(GM/r^2)\,\Delta r = -2GM R/d^3$ — a binomial expansion in disguise. Numerically $2(6.674\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})(6.37\times10^{6})/(3.84\times10^{8})^3 = 1.10\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, about $10^{-7}$ of $g$.

name: When does mgh stop working?
statement: The exact gravitational potential energy is $U = -GM_Em/r$. Rising a height $h$ from the surface changes it by $\Delta U = GM_Em\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{R+h}\right)$. Expanding in $h/R$ gives $\Delta U \approx mgh(1 - h/R)$. For $h = 10.0$ km and $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, by what percent does $mgh$ overestimate the true energy change?
solution: Factor the exact expression as $\frac{GM_Em h}{R^2}\left(1+h/R\right)^{-1} \approx mgh(1-h/R)$. The fractional overestimate of $mgh$ is therefore just $h/R = 10.0/6370 = 1.57\times10^{-3}$, or $0.157\%$. This is why $mgh$ is safe for laboratory heights and unsafe for orbits.

name: Precision of a g measurement
statement: A student finds $g$ from $g = 4\pi^2 L/T^2$. The length is known to $\pm 0.20\%$ and the period to $\pm 0.10\%$. Using a first-order Taylor expansion to propagate the errors (worst case, adding magnitudes), what is the percent uncertainty in $g$?
solution: For a product of powers, $\frac{\delta g}{g} = \frac{\delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\delta T}{T}$ — each exponent multiplies its fractional error. That gives $0.20\% + 2(0.10\%) = 0.40\%$. The period matters twice as much per percent, which is why one times many swings at once.

name: Deviation by a thin prism
statement: A thin glass prism has apex angle $A = 5.0^\circ$ and index $n = 1.52$. For small angles, applying $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ at both faces gives a deviation $\delta = (n-1)A$. Find $\delta$ in degrees.
solution: At each face Snell's law linearizes to $\theta_1 = n\theta_2$, and the geometry gives total deviation $\delta = \theta_1+\theta_1' - A$. Combining with $\theta_2+\theta_2' = A$ yields $\delta = (n-1)A$, independent of how the ray enters. Numerically $\delta = 0.52 \times 5.0^\circ = 2.6^\circ$.

name: Sag of a nearly straight cable
statement: A uniform cable of linear density $1.5$ kg/m is strung horizontally across a $40.0$ m span under a tension of $5.0\times10^{3}$ N. For small sag the catenary reduces to the parabola $y = \mu g x^2/(2T)$ measured from the lowest point. Find the sag at the center, in meters.
solution: Expanding $\cosh(\mu g x/T)\approx 1+\frac{1}{2}(\mu g x/T)^2$ turns the catenary into a parabola whenever the sag is small compared with the span. With $x = 20.0$ m (half the span), $s = (1.5)(9.8)(20.0)^2/(2\times5.0\times10^3) = 0.588$ m. The sag is $1.5\%$ of the span, so the approximation is excellent.

name: Raising a satellite by ten kilometers
statement: A satellite orbits at an altitude of $400$ km ($r = 6.77\times10^{6}$ m), where its period is $5.54\times10^{3}$ s. Kepler's third law gives $T \propto r^{3/2}$. Use the binomial approximation to find how much the period increases if the orbital radius is raised by $10.0$ km, in seconds.
solution: $T \propto r^{3/2}$ implies $\Delta T/T \approx \frac{3}{2}\Delta r/r$. Here $\Delta r/r = 10.0/6770 = 1.477\times10^{-3}$, so $\Delta T/T = 2.216\times10^{-3}$ and $\Delta T = (5.54\times10^3)(2.216\times10^{-3}) = 12.3$ s. Recomputing the period exactly gives the same value.

name: Redshift of a receding star
statement: A star recedes at $v = 3.00\times10^{5}$ m/s. For $v \ll c$ the relativistic Doppler formula reduces to $\Delta\lambda/\lambda \approx v/c$. Find the shift of the hydrogen line at $\lambda = 656.3$ nm, in nanometers. Take $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: $\lambda' = \lambda\sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} \approx \lambda(1+\beta)$ once both square roots are expanded to first order. With $\beta = 1.00\times10^{-3}$, $\Delta\lambda = (656.3)(1.00\times10^{-3}) = 0.656$ nm. The second-order term would add only about $3\times10^{-4}$ nm.

name: Length contraction of an airliner
statement: An airliner of proper length $60.0$ m flies at $250$ m/s. Using $\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2} \approx 1-\frac{v^2}{2c^2}$, find how much shorter it is in the ground frame, in meters. Take $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: The contraction is $\Delta L = L\left(1-\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\right) \approx L\beta^2/2$. With $\beta^2 = (250/3.00\times10^8)^2 = 6.94\times10^{-13}$, $\Delta L = (60.0)(3.47\times10^{-13}) = 2.08\times10^{-11}$ m — smaller than an atom. Trying to evaluate $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ on a calculator directly would return exactly 1.

name: Pressure one hundred meters up
statement: In an isothermal atmosphere $p = p_0 e^{-h/H}$ with scale height $H = 8500$ m. Take $p_0 = 101.3$ kPa and use $e^{-x} \approx 1-x$ to estimate the pressure at the top of a $100$ m tower, in kilopascals.
solution: For $h \ll H$ the exponential is linear, $p \approx p_0(1-h/H)$, which is just the hydrostatic result $p_0 - \rho g h$. With $h/H = 0.01176$, $p \approx 101.3(1-0.01176) = 100.1$ kPa. The exact exponential gives $100.12$ kPa.

name: Field of a distant dipole
statement: Two charges $+2.0$ nC and $-2.0$ nC are separated by $2.0$ mm along the $x$-axis. On the axis at $x = 0.50$ m from the center, expanding $\frac{1}{(x\mp d/2)^2}$ in powers of $d/x$ gives $E \approx \frac{2kp}{x^3}$ with $p = qd$. Compute $E$ in N/C, using $k = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$.
solution: The monopole terms cancel exactly, so the leading surviving term comes from the first-order binomial expansion, and the field falls off as $1/x^3$ rather than $1/x^2$. With $p = (2.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 4.0\times10^{-12}$ C\,m, $E = 2(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-12})/(0.50)^3 = 0.575$ N/C.

name: Pendulum clock in a warm room
statement: A pendulum clock with a brass rod ($\alpha = 1.9\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$) is calibrated at $20^\circ$C. The room warms to $35^\circ$C. Using $T \propto L^{1/2}$ and the binomial approximation, how many seconds does the clock lose in one day?
solution: $\Delta L/L = \alpha\Delta T$, and the half-power gives $\Delta T/T = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta T$. That is $\frac{1}{2}(1.9\times10^{-5})(15) = 1.425\times10^{-4}$. Over $86400$ s the clock falls behind by $(1.425\times10^{-4})(86400) = 12.3$ s.

name: Amplitude correction to a pendulum clock
statement: The period of a pendulum swung to amplitude $\theta_0$ is $T = T_0\left(1+\frac{\theta_0^2}{16}+\dots\right)$, where $T_0 = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ is the small-angle result. A clock is regulated assuming $T_0$ but actually swings to $\theta_0 = 20^\circ$. How many seconds does it lose per day?
solution: The leading correction is quadratic in amplitude, so it comes from the $\theta^3$ term of $\sin\theta$ that the small-angle approximation throws away. With $\theta_0 = 0.3491$ rad, $\theta_0^2/16 = 7.615\times10^{-3}$. Over $86400$ s that is $(7.615\times10^{-3})(86400) = 658$ s, about eleven minutes — small-angle errors are not always small.

name: Vibration frequency in a Lennard-Jones well
statement: Two atoms interact through $U(r) = U_0\left[\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^{12}-2\left(\frac{a}{r}\right)^{6}\right]$, which has its minimum at $r = a$. Expanding $U$ to second order about $r = a$ gives an effective spring constant $k = 72U_0/a^2$. For $U_0 = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J, $a = 3.0\times10^{-10}$ m, and reduced mass $m = 1.0\times10^{-26}$ kg, find the angular frequency of small vibrations, in rad/s.
solution: Near a minimum every potential looks like a parabola: $U \approx U_{\min} + \frac{1}{2}U''(a)(r-a)^2$, so $k = U''(a)$. Differentiating twice gives $U''(a) = 72U_0/a^2 = 72(1.6\times10^{-19})/(9.0\times10^{-20}) = 128$ N/m. Then $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{128/1.0\times10^{-26}} = 1.13\times10^{14}$ rad/s, an infrared vibration.

name: Height of the equilibrium tide
statement: Balancing the Moon's tidal potential against Earth's own gravity gives an equilibrium tidal bulge of height $h = \frac{3}{2}\frac{M_m}{M_E}\frac{R^4}{d^3}$. With $M_m = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg, $M_E = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg, $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, and $d = 3.84\times10^{8}$ m, compute $h$ in meters.
solution: The tidal potential is the second-order term left over after expanding $-GM_m/|\vec{d}-\vec{r}|$ in powers of $R/d$; setting that equal to $gh$ on Earth's surface gives the formula above. Numerically $\frac{3}{2}(0.01231)(1.647\times10^{27})/(5.66\times10^{25}) = 0.54$ m. Real tides differ from this because ocean basins resonate.

name: Tidal stretch on an astronaut
statement: An astronaut of height $1.8$ m floats in a spacecraft at orbital radius $r = 6.77\times10^{6}$ m, oriented radially. Using the first-order expansion of $GM_E/r^2$, find the difference in gravitational acceleration between the astronaut's head and feet, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Take $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$.
solution: Differentiate the field rather than subtracting two nearly equal numbers: $|\Delta a| = \frac{2GM_E}{r^3}\Delta r$. With $\Delta r = 1.8$ m, $|\Delta a| = 2(3.986\times10^{14})(1.8)/(3.10\times10^{20}) = 4.6\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Subtracting the two accelerations directly would lose all significant figures on a calculator.

name: Counting Newton's rings
statement: A plano-convex lens of radius of curvature $2.00$ m rests on a flat glass plate. The air gap a distance $r$ from the contact point is $t = r^2/2R$, which follows from expanding $R-\sqrt{R^2-r^2}$. Illuminated from above with $589$ nm light, how many dark rings appear within a radius of $1.00$ cm? Give an integer.
solution: $\sqrt{R^2-r^2} = R\sqrt{1-r^2/R^2} \approx R(1-r^2/2R^2)$, so the gap is $t = r^2/2R$. Dark rings occur where $2t = m\lambda$, i.e. $m = r^2/(R\lambda)$. At $r = 1.00$ cm, $t = 2.50\times10^{-5}$ m and $m = 2t/\lambda = 84.9$, so $84$ complete dark rings fit inside.

name: How large an amplitude is still small?
statement: Using $T = T_0(1+\theta_0^2/16)$, find the largest amplitude for which the small-angle period is accurate to $0.10\%$. Give the answer in degrees.
solution: Set the fractional error equal to the tolerance: $\theta_0^2/16 = 1.0\times10^{-3}$, so $\theta_0 = \sqrt{0.016} = 0.1265$ rad. Converting, $\theta_0 = 7.2^\circ$. This is the practical rule that pendulum swings under roughly $7^\circ$ are isochronous to a part in a thousand.

name: Why GPS clocks need a correction
statement: A GPS satellite orbits at $r = 2.656\times10^{7}$ m. Two first-order effects shift its clock rate relative to a clock on Earth's surface ($R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m): the gravitational shift $\frac{GM_E}{c^2}\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{r}\right)$ makes it run fast, and the kinematic shift $\frac{v^2}{2c^2}$ with $v^2 = GM_E/r$ makes it run slow. Find the net time the satellite clock gains per day, in microseconds. Use $GM_E = 3.986\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $c = 3.00\times10^{8}$ m/s.
solution: Both effects are first-order expansions of square roots in $\Phi/c^2$ and $v^2/c^2$, so they simply add. The gravitational term is $5.285\times10^{-10}$ and the kinematic term is $8.34\times10^{-11}$, giving a net fractional rate of $4.45\times10^{-10}$. Over $86400$ s that is $(4.45\times10^{-10})(86400) = 38.5\ \mu$s — uncorrected, this would push GPS positions off by more than $10$ km per day.

name: Deflection of a plumb line by Earth's rotation
statement: Because Earth rotates, a plumb bob at latitude $\lambda$ hangs slightly off the true radial direction. The centrifugal acceleration $\omega^2R\cos\lambda$ has a horizontal component $\omega^2R\cos\lambda\sin\lambda$, and for a small deflection $\tan\delta \approx \delta$. Find the deflection at $\lambda = 45^\circ$, in degrees. Take $\omega = 7.292\times10^{-5}$ rad/s, $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The deflection satisfies $\tan\delta = \frac{\omega^2R\sin\lambda\cos\lambda}{g}$, and at $45^\circ$ the product $\sin\lambda\cos\lambda = 1/2$. Then $\delta \approx \omega^2R/(2g) = (5.317\times10^{-9})(6.37\times10^{6})/19.6 = 1.728\times10^{-3}$ rad. Converting, $\delta = 0.099^\circ$, or about $6$ arcminutes — the maximum anywhere on Earth.

name: Tilted Axes on a Frictionless Incline
statement: A $2.0\,\text{kg}$ block slides on a frictionless incline of angle $\theta = 30^\circ$. Find the magnitude of its acceleration along the incline, in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Tilt the axes so $x$ points down the slope. Then the normal force has no $x$ component and the motion is one-dimensional in $x$. Newton's law along the slope gives $ma = mg\sin\theta$, so $a = g\sin 30^\circ = 4.9\,\text{m/s}^2$. The mass cancels, which is the usual sign that the axis choice was right.

name: Normal Force with Tilted Axes
statement: The same $2.0\,\text{kg}$ block sits on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline. Using axes along and perpendicular to the surface, find the normal force in $\text{N}$.
solution: Perpendicular to the incline there is no acceleration, because the block moves along the surface. So $N - mg\cos\theta = 0$, giving $N = (2.0)(9.8)\cos 30^\circ = 17\,\text{N}$. With horizontal-vertical axes you would need both components of $\vec a$ and get the same answer with more algebra.

name: Two Blocks as One System
statement: Blocks of mass $3.0\,\text{kg}$ and $5.0\,\text{kg}$ sit touching each other on a frictionless horizontal table. A horizontal force of $12\,\text{N}$ pushes on the $3.0\,\text{kg}$ block, so both slide together. Find the acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Treat the two blocks as a single system. The contact force between them is internal and drops out, so $F = (m_1+m_2)a$ and $a = 12/8.0 = 1.5\,\text{m/s}^2$.

name: Isolating the Second Block
statement: For the same two blocks ($3.0\,\text{kg}$ in front of a $5.0\,\text{kg}$ block, $12\,\text{N}$ applied to the $3.0\,\text{kg}$ one, frictionless table), find the magnitude of the contact force between the blocks, in $\text{N}$.
solution: To expose an internal force you must isolate one body. The $5.0\,\text{kg}$ block feels only the contact force $F_c$, so $F_c = (5.0)(1.5) = 7.5\,\text{N}$. Isolating the $3.0\,\text{kg}$ block instead gives $12 - F_c = (3.0)(1.5)$, the same result.

name: Atwood Machine Acceleration
statement: An ideal pulley carries a light string with $3.0\,\text{kg}$ on one side and $5.0\,\text{kg}$ on the other. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of either block, in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Because the string is inextensible, unroll the system into one line of mass $m_1+m_2$ driven by the net weight $(m_2-m_1)g$. Then $a = (5.0-3.0)(9.8)/8.0 = 2.45\,\text{m/s}^2$, and the tension never appears.

name: Atwood Tension by Isolation
statement: For the $3.0\,\text{kg}$ / $5.0\,\text{kg}$ Atwood machine above, find the string tension in $\text{N}$.
solution: Tension is internal to the whole system, so isolate one block. For the rising $3.0\,\text{kg}$ block, $T - m_1 g = m_1 a$, giving $T = 3.0(9.8+2.45) = 36.8\,\text{N}$. Check: $T$ lies between $m_1g = 29.4\,\text{N}$ and $m_2g = 49\,\text{N}$, as it must.

name: Field at the Midpoint of Two Equal Charges
statement: Two identical point charges $q = +4.0\,\text{nC}$ are held $6.0\,\text{cm}$ apart. Find the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint of the line joining them, in $\text{N/C}$.
solution: The setup is unchanged if you reflect it through the midpoint, but that reflection reverses any field vector there. A vector equal to its own negative is zero, so $E = 0$. No calculation is needed.

name: Scale Reading in an Accelerating Elevator
statement: A $60\,\text{kg}$ person stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $2.0\,\text{m/s}^2$. Find the scale reading in $\text{N}$.
solution: Work in the ground frame with $+y$ up and isolate the person. Then $N - mg = ma$, so $N = 60(9.8+2.0) = 708\,\text{N}$. Limiting check: with $a=0$ this returns $588\,\text{N}$, the person's weight.

name: Balanced Wheatstone Bridge
statement: A bridge has $10\,\Omega$ and $20\,\Omega$ in series on the left branch, $10\,\Omega$ and $20\,\Omega$ in series on the right branch, and a $50\,\Omega$ resistor connecting the two midpoints. A $12\,\text{V}$ battery is across the outer terminals. Find the current in the $50\,\Omega$ bridge resistor, in $\text{A}$.
solution: The two branches are identical, so the two midpoints divide the same voltage in the same ratio and sit at equal potential. With no potential difference across it, the bridge resistor carries zero current.

name: Choosing the Pivot on a Loaded Plank
statement: A uniform $20\,\text{kg}$ plank of length $4.0\,\text{m}$ rests on supports at its two ends. A $50\,\text{kg}$ person stands $1.0\,\text{m}$ from the left end. Find the upward force from the right support, in $\text{N}$.
solution: Take torques about the left support, which kills the unknown left reaction. Then $N_R(4.0) = (20)(9.8)(2.0) + (50)(9.8)(1.0) = 882\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, so $N_R = 220\,\text{N}$. The person is nearer the left support, so the right support should carry less than half the total weight of $686\,\text{N}$; it does.

name: Ring of Charge on Its Axis
statement: A thin ring of radius $R = 0.10\,\text{m}$ carries a uniformly distributed charge $Q = 5.0\,\text{nC}$. Find the magnitude of the electric field on the axis at distance $z = 0.10\,\text{m}$ from the center, in $\text{N/C}$. Use $k = 8.99\times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$.
solution: Rotational symmetry about the axis means the components perpendicular to the axis from opposite bits of the ring cancel, so only the axial component survives. Each element contributes $k\,dq/(z^2+R^2)$ times the factor $z/\sqrt{z^2+R^2}$, and every element has the same distance, so $$E = \frac{kQz}{(z^2+R^2)^{3/2}} = 1.59\times 10^3\,\text{N/C}.$$

name: Wedge Accelerated So the Block Does Not Slide
statement: A block rests on the frictionless $25^\circ$ face of a wedge. The wedge is pushed horizontally so that the block stays at rest relative to the wedge. Find the required acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Use horizontal and vertical axes here, not tilted ones, because the acceleration is horizontal. Vertically $N\cos\theta = mg$; horizontally $N\sin\theta = ma$. Dividing gives $a = g\tan 25^\circ = 4.57\,\text{m/s}^2$. Limiting check: $\theta \to 0$ gives $a \to 0$.

name: Normal Force on the Accelerating Wedge
statement: For the same $25^\circ$ frictionless wedge accelerating so that a $1.5\,\text{kg}$ block rides along without sliding, find the normal force on the block in $\text{N}$.
solution: The vertical equation alone fixes $N$, since the block has no vertical acceleration: $N\cos\theta = mg$, so $N = (1.5)(9.8)/\cos 25^\circ = 16.2\,\text{N}$. It exceeds $mg = 14.7\,\text{N}$ because the surface must also supply the horizontal push.

name: Pulley with Friction: System First
statement: A $4.0\,\text{kg}$ block on a horizontal table is connected over an ideal pulley at the table edge to a $3.0\,\text{kg}$ hanging block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between block and table is $0.25$. Find the magnitude of the acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Take both blocks plus string as one system moving with common speed. The driving force is the hanging weight $m_2 g$, the retarding force is friction $\mu m_1 g$, and the tension is internal: $$a = \frac{m_2 g - \mu m_1 g}{m_1+m_2} = \frac{29.4-9.8}{7.0} = 2.8\,\text{m/s}^2.$$

name: Tension in the Friction Pulley Problem
statement: For the setup above ($4.0\,\text{kg}$ on the table with $\mu_k = 0.25$, $3.0\,\text{kg}$ hanging), find the string tension in $\text{N}$.
solution: Isolate the hanging block. Then $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$, so $T = 3.0(9.8-2.8) = 21\,\text{N}$. Isolating the table block gives $T - \mu m_1 g = m_1 a$, i.e. $9.8 + 11.2 = 21\,\text{N}$, a useful cross-check.

name: Cube of Resistors: Body Diagonal
statement: Twelve identical $6.0\,\Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube. Find the resistance between two opposite corners of the cube (a body diagonal), in $\Omega$.
solution: Symmetry about the body diagonal makes the three corners next to the input equipotential, and likewise the three next to the output. Merging equipotential nodes turns the cube into three resistors in parallel, then six, then three: $$R = \frac{R_0}{3}+\frac{R_0}{6}+\frac{R_0}{3} = \frac{5R_0}{6} = 5.0\,\Omega.$$

name: Infinite Ladder Network
statement: An infinite ladder is built from $1.0\,\Omega$ resistors: a series $1.0\,\Omega$ into a node, a $1.0\,\Omega$ shunt to the bottom rail, then the pattern repeats forever. Find the input resistance in $\Omega$.
solution: The ladder is self-similar, so removing one stage leaves the same network of resistance $R$. Then $R = 1 + \dfrac{1\cdot R}{1+R}$, i.e. $R^2 - R - 1 = 0$, so $R = (1+\sqrt 5)/2 = 1.62\,\Omega$. The negative root is discarded as unphysical.

name: Elastic Collision via the CM Frame
statement: A $2.0\,\text{kg}$ ball moving at $+5.0\,\text{m/s}$ collides head-on and elastically with a stationary $3.0\,\text{kg}$ ball. Find the velocity of the $2.0\,\text{kg}$ ball afterward, in $\text{m/s}$ (sign included, with $+$ along the initial motion).
solution: In the center-of-mass frame an elastic head-on collision simply reverses each velocity. Here $v_{cm} = (2)(5)/5 = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$, so the light ball approaches the CM at $+3.0$ and leaves at $-3.0$; back in the lab frame that is $2.0-3.0 = -1.0\,\text{m/s}$. It rebounds because the target is heavier.

name: Energy Method on a Rough Incline
statement: A block is released from rest and slides $3.0\,\text{m}$ down a $30^\circ$ incline with coefficient of kinetic friction $0.20$. Find its speed at the bottom, in $\text{m/s}$.
solution: Energy accounting avoids solving for the acceleration and then the kinematics. Gravity does $mgL\sin\theta$ and friction removes $\mu mgL\cos\theta$, so $$v = \sqrt{2gL(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)} = 4.38\,\text{m/s}.$$ The mass cancels, as it must for a problem with only gravity and dry friction.

name: Fixing an Unknown Coefficient by a Limiting Case
statement: A student derives the Atwood acceleration as $a = \dfrac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1 + n\,m_2}$ but cannot remember the number $n$. Determine $n$ by taking the limit $m_1 \to 0$, where the remaining block must fall freely, then evaluate $a$ for $m_1 = 6.0\,\text{kg}$ and $m_2 = 4.0\,\text{kg}$. Give the magnitude of $a$ in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: A limiting case can pin down a forgotten constant. Setting $m_1 = 0$ gives $a = -g/n$, and free fall requires magnitude $g$, so $n = 1$. Then $a = (2.0)(9.8)/10.0 = 1.96\,\text{m/s}^2$.

name: Speed of a Point on a Rolling Wheel
statement: A wheel of radius $0.35\,\text{m}$ rolls without slipping with center speed $3.0\,\text{m/s}$. Find the ground-frame speed of the point on the rim level with the axle (a quarter turn from the contact point), in $\text{m/s}$.
solution: Rolling motion is translation of the center plus rotation about it, and the two contributions at this point are perpendicular: $v_{cm}$ forward and $\omega R = v_{cm}$ vertical. So $v = \sqrt 2\,(3.0) = 4.24\,\text{m/s}$. Equivalently, the contact point is instantaneously at rest and this point is $\sqrt 2 R$ from it.

name: Pendulum in an Accelerating Train
statement: A small bob hangs from the ceiling of a train accelerating horizontally at $2.5\,\text{m/s}^2$. In the steady state, find the angle the string makes with the vertical, in degrees.
solution: In the train frame add a pseudo-force $ma$ opposite the acceleration; the bob then hangs along the effective gravity $\vec g_{\text{eff}}$. Its tilt is $\theta = \arctan(a/g) = \arctan(2.5/9.8) = 14.3^\circ$. Limiting check: $a \to 0$ gives a vertical string.

name: Cube of Resistors: Face Diagonal
statement: Twelve identical $8.0\,\Omega$ resistors form the edges of a cube. Find the resistance between two corners on the same face that are diagonally opposite (a face diagonal), in $\Omega$.
solution: The mirror plane containing the two chosen corners forces symmetric pairs of nodes to sit at equal potential. Merging those pairs collapses the cube to a simple series-parallel network with $R = \tfrac{3}{4}R_0 = 6.0\,\Omega$. Sanity check: this is less than the body-diagonal value $\tfrac{5}{6}R_0 = 6.7\,\Omega$, as it should be for corners that are closer together.

name: Uniform Sphere with an Off-Center Cavity
statement: A sphere of radius $R = 0.10\,\text{m}$ carries uniform charge density $\rho = 2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{C/m}^3$, except for an empty spherical cavity of radius $R/2$ whose center is $d = 0.050\,\text{m}$ from the sphere's center. Find the magnitude of the electric field inside the cavity, in $\text{N/C}$. Use $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$.
solution: Superpose a full sphere of density $+\rho$ with a small sphere of density $-\rho$ at the cavity's center. Inside a uniform sphere $\vec E = \rho\vec r/(3\varepsilon_0)$ measured from its own center, so the two position-dependent terms cancel and leave the constant field $$E = \frac{\rho d}{3\varepsilon_0} = 3.76\times10^3\,\text{N/C}.$$ The field in the cavity is uniform, which no direct integration would reveal so cheaply.

name: Ladder Against a Frictionless Wall
statement: A uniform ladder leans at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal against a frictionless vertical wall, with friction only at the floor. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction at the floor for the ladder not to slip. Answer is dimensionless.
solution: Take torques about the base, which eliminates both floor forces at once and leaves only the wall force $N_w$ and the weight. That gives $N_w L\sin\theta = mg(L/2)\cos\theta$, so $N_w = \tfrac12 mg\cot\theta$. Horizontal balance requires friction $f = N_w$ with $N_{\text{floor}} = mg$, hence $\mu_{\min} = \tfrac12\cot 60^\circ = 0.289$.

name: Block Sliding on a Free Wedge
statement: A $1.0\,\text{kg}$ block slides down the frictionless $30^\circ$ face of a $4.0\,\text{kg}$ wedge that is itself free to slide on a frictionless floor. Find the magnitude of the wedge's acceleration, in $\text{m/s}^2$.
solution: Horizontal momentum of the block-plus-wedge system is conserved, so work with the system horizontally and with the block in the wedge frame along the incline. The standard result is $$A = \frac{mg\sin\theta\cos\theta}{M+m\sin^2\theta} = \frac{(1.0)(9.8)(0.5)(0.866)}{4.0+0.25} = 1.0\,\text{m/s}^2.$$ Limiting check: $M\to\infty$ gives $A\to 0$, the fixed-wedge case.

name: Energy Lost in a Perfectly Inelastic Collision
statement: A $2.0\,\text{kg}$ cart moving at $6.0\,\text{m/s}$ strikes and sticks to a stationary $4.0\,\text{kg}$ cart on a frictionless track. Find the kinetic energy converted to other forms, in $\text{J}$.
solution: In the CM frame the final state is at rest, so exactly the CM-frame kinetic energy is lost. That energy is $\tfrac12 \mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$ with reduced mass $\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2) = 4/3\,\text{kg}$: $$\Delta E = \tfrac12(4/3)(6.0)^2 = 24\,\text{J}.$$ Note that only the relative velocity matters, never the frame you happen to watch from.

name: Flux Through One Face from a Corner Charge
statement: A point charge $q = 6.0\,\mu\text{C}$ sits at one corner of a cube. Find the electric flux through one of the three faces that do not touch that corner, in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}$. Use $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$.
solution: Build a big cube of eight copies with the charge at its center. By symmetry each of the six big faces takes $q/(6\varepsilon_0)$, and each big face is made of four of the small faces in question, so one small face gets $q/(24\varepsilon_0) = 2.82\times10^4\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}$. The three faces touching the charge get zero flux, since the field is parallel to them.

name: Infinite Grid of Resistors
statement: An infinite square lattice of nodes is wired with a $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor along every edge. Find the resistance between two adjacent nodes, in $\Omega$.
solution: Inject current $I$ at node $A$ alone; by fourfold symmetry $I/4$ leaves along each of its four edges. Separately extract $I$ at the neighbor $B$ alone; again $I/4$ flows into $B$ along the connecting edge. Superposing the two problems is exactly the physical situation, and the shared edge carries $I/2$, so $V_{AB} = (I/2)R_0$ and $R_{AB} = R_0/2 = 1.5\,\Omega$.

name: Cheapest Angle to Drag a Block Uphill
statement: A $5.0\,\text{kg}$ block is dragged at constant speed up a $25^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.35$. The applied force may point at any angle above the incline surface. Find the smallest force magnitude that works, in $\text{N}$.
solution: Tilt the axes to the incline and let the force make angle $\alpha$ with the surface. Then $F\cos\alpha = mg\sin\theta + \mu(mg\cos\theta - F\sin\alpha)$, so $$F = \frac{mg(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)}{\cos\alpha+\mu\sin\alpha}.$$ The denominator is maximal when $\tan\alpha = \mu$ (here $\alpha = 19.3^\circ$), where it equals $\sqrt{1+\mu^2}$, giving $F_{\min} = 34.2\,\text{N}$. Limiting check: with $\mu=0$ the best angle is along the incline and $F = mg\sin\theta$.

name: Acceleration from a velocity-time graph
statement: A glider on an air track is tracked by a motion sensor. Its velocity-time graph is a straight line rising from $2.0$ m/s at $t = 0$ to $14.0$ m/s at $t = 4.0$ s. What is the acceleration of the glider, in m/s$^2$?
